source.title: Flatness Improves Backbone Generalisation in Few-Shot Classification
source.authors: Rui Li; Martin Trapp; Marcus Klasson; Arno Solin

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices; no material cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAM-based flatness-seeking training changes few-shot classification performance on seen and unseen domains, extending flatness/generalization results to a multi-domain few-shot classification setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAM-versus-ERM results on Meta-Dataset for multiple datasets and adaptation methods, Hessian flatness measures, and a ViT experiment. Fine-tuning, fusion-method, and state-of-the-art comparisons are included only where they bear on the claim's flatness/generalization or measured-flatness versions. Cited prior findings are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness–generalization connection to motivate SAM and evaluates its own few-shot classification pipeline. It does not test V7's correlation between magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and train–test error gaps: it measures unscaled Hessian curvature and query accuracy, without measured training errors, matched low training losses, or comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: flatness-seeking backbone training can improve few-shot classification, and their SAM-plus-fine-tuning pipeline outperforms prior methods on 10 of 13 Meta-Dataset domains. They acknowledge benchmark limitations and extra training cost. This is a conclusion about SAM-based training and transfer accuracy, not evidence for V7's specific magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap correlation.
record.recipe_differences: Tests SAM versus ERM backbone training in multi-domain few-shot classification using Meta-Dataset, with adapted few-shot evaluation and Hessian-based flatness measures; does not test the original versions' random-label, width, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, or memorized-example setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by adaptation method (SUR versus TSA), dataset/domain (seen versus unseen), and backbone architecture (ResNet-18 versus ViT-small).

fits_no_version.finding: With ResNet-18, SAM raises TSA average seen/unseen query accuracy from 75.99/76.84 to 77.67/78.56. With SUR, seen accuracy rises from 77.58 to 78.71 while unseen accuracy falls from 63.71 to 63.34.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM backbone training can improve few-shot classification accuracy, with benefits dependent on adaptation method and domain.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM lowers both Hessian trace and top eigenvalue on six of eight training datasets, but raises both on ILSVRC 2012 and CU Birds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM often reduces unscaled Hessian curvature of trained backbones, but does not do so uniformly across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM fine-tuning improves ViT-small query accuracy on the recorded datasets except DTD, where the reported accuracies are identical.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM fine-tuning can improve pretrained vision-transformer performance in few-shot classification.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Workshop/Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision, 2024
record.problems: Evidence is limited to the Meta-Dataset benchmark, whose authors say its datasets are mostly natural images, black-and-white drawings, or written characters and whose unseen domains are close to seen domains. No direct train-test error gap is reported. They note SAM's additional computational training cost. Some Hessian measures contradict the overall flatness tendency on ILSVRC 2012 and CU Birds; results use mini-batches, for which cited theoretical results do not apply.
record.rows_left_out: None; all separately reported Table 1 comparisons for ERM versus SAM and b-SAM, Table 3 trace and top-eigenvalue measurements, and Table 7 SAM versus ERM comparisons are represented. Fine-tuning and information-fusion comparisons are not separate claim-version rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out generalization under the same architecture and training recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets; SAM and ERM are objectives, and the main controlled comparison uses SGD for both.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty; differing recipe hyperparameters are not a controlled batch-size test.
Dropout interventions, small-data regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance correlated with measured train–test error gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Hessian curvature and few-shot accuracy do not establish this relationship.
Removal of examples selected by label memorization versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to the supplied versions; the numerical method comparisons remain readable. Theorem 3.2 bounds target excess risk relative to optimal target risk using source objectives, domain discrepancy, and complexity terms; it does not establish V7. The record's coverage statement is inaccurate: Table 7 also reports MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and averages, and Table 1 includes individual b-SAM comparisons omitted from the rows. These omissions do not bear on any supplied version, so they are not claim-relevant missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test generalization under the same architecture and training recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and corresponding test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparisons.
Large versus small batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.

The paper tests SAM versus ERM in few-shot classification, reporting Hessian trace and top eigenvalues as flatness measures. It does not test magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, ranking against norm- and margin-based measures, or the stated CIFAR-10/SVHN setting without augmentation.
Removal of memorized training examples and its effect on test accuracy.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-18 evaluated with TSA on Meta-Dataset
reader_labels.reason: SAM improves average seen and unseen accuracy versus ERM (R29–R30), and the authors report better averages for both domains.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ViT-small with Prototype classifier on Meta-Dataset
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports higher average accuracy for SAM than ERM on both seen and unseen sets (R51–R60; Table 7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-18 evaluated with SUR, especially unseen domains
reader_labels.reason: SAM improves average seen accuracy but average unseen accuracy is lower; three individual unseen datasets also decline (R14–R15, R10–R13).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Hessian flatness metrics across ResNet-18 training datasets
reader_labels.reason: SAM lowers trace and top eigenvalue in most reported datasets, but both measures are higher for ILSVRC 2012 and CU Birds (R35–R50).
